course.title: SQL
course.description: A research-grounded SQL course progressing from relational modeling and table design through querying, joins, aggregation, window functions, transactions, concurrency, reusable database logic, performance tuning, security, testing, recovery, partitioning, and a realistic capstone. Portable SQL concepts are taught first; PostgreSQL 18 is the reference execution dialect for advanced labs and implementation-specific features are clearly identified.
prerequisites: Ability to read simple tabular data
learningOutcomes: Design relational tables with appropriate keys and integrity constraints.
Write accurate SQL for filtering, sorting, pagination, joins, subqueries, set operations, and CTEs.
Build grouped and windowed analytics at a defined data grain.
Modify data safely and design atomic transactions.
Reason about isolation levels, locking, serialization failures, and retry behavior.
Use views, routines, and triggers appropriately while identifying implementation-specific behavior.
Diagnose SQL performance using indexes and execution plans.
Prevent SQL injection with parameterization and apply least privilege.
Create repeatable SQL tests and reason about backup, migration, and partitioning practices.
Deliver and explain a complete SQL system with schema, data, analytics, security, and performance evidence.

modules.title: SQL Foundations and Relational Thinking
modules.description: Establish SQL terminology, relational modeling, reproducible practice, and query reasoning.

lessons.title: SQL, Relational Databases, and Standards
lessons.description: Understand SQL as a standardized language used by relational database systems, while recognizing that PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite implement different subsets and extensions.
learningObjectives: Define SQL, relation, tuple/row, attribute/column, key, and constraint.
Explain why SQL portability is limited by vendor-specific features.

notes.text: Portable core

The ISO/IEC 9075 family specifies SQL. A database product implements that language and may add extensions or omit features. The course therefore teaches standard concepts first and uses PostgreSQL 18 as the reference implementation for advanced labs.

items: Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys express relationships.
SQL result sets are unordered unless an ORDER BY clause requests an order.
NULL participates in three-valued logic; it is not an ordinary value.

notes.text: Do not memorize a product-specific syntax as though it were universal SQL.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes SQL?
options: A server product made by PostgreSQL
A standardized language implemented by database products
quiz.answer: A standardized language implemented by database products
quiz.explanation: SQL is standardized; products implement it with varying feature sets and extensions.

summary: SQL is a standardized language family, not one database product.
Relational concepts are the foundation for later query and integrity work.

lessons.title: Keys, Relationships, and Data Grain
lessons.description: Learn to translate business entities and relationships into relational tables before writing queries.
learningObjectives: Choose primary keys from candidate identifiers.
Model one-to-many and many-to-many relationships.
State the grain of a table or query result before calculating measures.

notes.text: If customers place orders and orders contain products, a customer-to-order relationship is one-to-many and order-to-product is many-to-many. A junction table such as order_item carries one row per order/product pairing and can store quantity or line price.

items: Grain answers “one row represents what?”
Incorrect grain is a major source of double-counted reports.

quiz.question: Where should quantity normally live in an order/product many-to-many model?
quiz.explanation: Quantity describes the relationship between one order and one product, so it belongs at the junction-row grain.

summary: Business rules should drive relational structure.
State row grain explicitly before joining or aggregating.

lessons.title: SQL Clients, Scripts, and Reproducible Labs
lessons.description: Create a repeatable local SQL workflow rather than depending on interactive GUI actions.
learningObjectives: Create a dedicated practice schema.
Execute SQL from scripts and record the target DB/version.
Separate schema setup, test data, queries, and teardown.

notes.text:
SELECT version();
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS training;

items: PostgreSQL is the reference lab dialect for advanced examples.
SQLite is lightweight but intentionally omits some features and adds its own behavior.
MySQL 8.4 is included as a dialect comparison point.

quiz.question: Why record the DBMS/version when testing SQL?
options: It is required for every SELECT
Implementations differ in supported features and behavior
quiz.answer: Implementations differ in supported features and behavior
quiz.explanation: The standard does not imply identical product behavior for every feature.

summary: Reproducibility comes from scripts and known execution contexts.
The database product/version is part of the meaning of a SQL test.

lessons.title: Statement Classes and Logical Query Order
lessons.description: Build the vocabulary and reasoning model used to read SQL statements.
learningObjectives: Classify DDL, DML, queries, transaction control, and access control statements.
Describe the logical order of common SELECT processing stages.

items: DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP define objects.
DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE modify data where supported.
Transaction control includes COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT in systems that support them.
FROM/JOIN form the source rows.
WHERE filters source rows.
GROUP BY forms groups; HAVING filters groups.
SELECT projects expressions.
ORDER BY orders the result.
FETCH/OFFSET or LIMIT limits rows.

notes.text: Logical query order explains semantics; it is not a promise about the physical execution plan.

quiz.question: Which clause filters rows before grouping?
quiz.explanation: WHERE filters source rows before GROUP BY creates groups.

summary: SQL statement families clarify intent.
Logical query order helps explain aliasing and aggregation rules.

tasks.title: Model a Retail Order Schema
tasks.description: Design a relational schema from a short business scenario.
tasks.problemStatement: Customers place orders; orders contain products; line quantity must be positive and every relationship must be valid.
requirements: PostgreSQL DDL or equivalent relational SQL.
hint: Put relationship attributes in the junction table.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The schema preserves relationships through foreign keys and prevents duplicate lines for the same order/product pair with a composite primary key.

modules.title: Data Definition and Integrity
modules.description: Define relational structures with appropriate types, constraints, schemas, views, and generated values.

lessons.title: CREATE TABLE and Data Types
lessons.description: Choose common SQL data types based on domain meaning, range, precision, and temporal semantics.
learningObjectives: Use CREATE TABLE with typed columns.
Choose exact numeric types for monetary values.
Explain why temporal types differ from plain strings.

items: NUMERIC/DECIMAL supports exact decimal arithmetic for values such as prices.
Character types, integer widths, boolean, and temporal types communicate domain intent.
Vendor-specific types should be isolated when portability matters.

quiz.question: Which type is designed for exact decimal arithmetic?
quiz.explanation: Exact numeric types are appropriate when decimal precision is part of the domain requirement.

summary: Type choice is a correctness decision, not only a storage decision.
Constraints complement types by expressing finer business rules.

lessons.title: Constraints and Referential Integrity
lessons.description: Turn data-quality rules into database-enforced guarantees.
learningObjectives: Use NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, CHECK, and FOREIGN KEY correctly.
Predict common constraint failures.
Choose ON DELETE behavior deliberately.

items: PRIMARY KEY identifies rows and is unique/non-null.
FOREIGN KEY protects referential relationships.
ON DELETE actions are domain choices; CASCADE can intentionally remove dependent rows but must be reviewed carefully.

quiz.question: What does a foreign key enforce?
quiz.explanation: A foreign key constrains values in a referencing table according to a referenced key.

summary: Constraints keep invalid states out of the database.
Referential actions should reflect the domain lifecycle.

lessons.title: ALTER, DROP, Schemas, and Migrations
lessons.description: Change database structure while preserving control over object names, dependencies, and deployment risk.
learningObjectives: Use ALTER TABLE for schema evolution.
Use schemas as namespaces.
Explain why destructive DDL needs a migration/recovery plan.

items: Schema-qualified names reduce ambiguity.
DROP ... CASCADE can remove dependent objects.
A migration should be versioned, reviewed, tested, and suitable for the target deployment process.

quiz.question: Why use schema-qualified names such as reporting.daily_sales?
options: To force a full table scan
To turn a table into JSON
quiz.explanation: Qualification identifies the intended namespace when multiple schemas are available.

summary: Schema evolution is part of database engineering.
Namespaces help organize objects and manage privileges.

lessons.title: Views and Generated Values
lessons.description: Use reusable query interfaces and modern generated-key patterns without confusing implementation features with the SQL core.
learningObjectives: Create a view.
Explain the role of generated identity values.
Distinguish normal views from materialized results.

notes.text: PostgreSQL normal views store the query definition rather than a physically materialized copy of the rows. Identity columns are a modern PostgreSQL mechanism for generated keys; other DBMSs use different syntax or facilities.

quiz.question: What does a normal PostgreSQL view primarily store?
quiz.explanation: A normal PostgreSQL view is a stored query definition evaluated when referenced.

summary: Views are reusable query interfaces.
Generated columns/values are implementation-sensitive and should be labeled when portability matters.

tasks.title: Harden an Order Schema
tasks.description: Add constraints that reject invalid orders.
tasks.problemStatement: Enforce required relationships, positive quantities, non-negative line prices, and allowed order states.
objectives: Add NOT NULL and UNIQUE rules.
requirements: Start with invariants rather than syntax.
PostgreSQL or equivalent SQL.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The constraints encode the most important integrity rules at the database boundary.

modules.title: Retrieval, Filtering, and Result Shaping
modules.description: Master projection, predicates, NULL handling, expressions, ordering, and reliable pagination.

lessons.title: Projection, Expressions, and DISTINCT
lessons.description: Write focused SELECT lists and calculated expressions.
learningObjectives: Select only needed columns.
Use aliases and expressions.
Explain DISTINCT as duplicate elimination over the projected row.

notes.text:
SELECT customer_name AS name,
       city,
       UPPER(city) AS normalized_city
FROM training.customers;

SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM training.customers
WHERE city IS NOT NULL;
SELECT * can make application interfaces unstable when table schemas evolve.

quiz.question: What does SELECT DISTINCT city remove?
options: Rows with duplicate city values in the result
quiz.answer: Rows with duplicate city values in the result
quiz.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows after projection.

summary: Projection shapes the result consumed by downstream users.
DISTINCT does not replace GROUP BY.

lessons.title: WHERE, NULL, and Boolean Logic
lessons.description: Filter correctly while understanding NULL and three-valued logic.
learningObjectives: Use IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL, AND, OR, and NOT.
Explain UNKNOWN in predicate evaluation.
Use parentheses to make compound conditions clear.

notes.text:
SELECT product_name
FROM training.products
WHERE (category = 'Accessories' OR category = 'Displays')
  AND unit_price BETWEEN 10.00 AND 50.00;

SELECT customer_name
FROM training.customers
WHERE city IS NULL;
Do not write city = NULL. NULL comparison results in UNKNOWN; use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

quiz.question: Which predicate correctly checks for NULL?
quiz.explanation: IS NULL is the SQL predicate for testing whether a value is NULL.

summary: WHERE predicates are evaluated with SQL Boolean semantics.
NULL requires explicit handling.

lessons.title: ORDER BY and Deterministic Pagination
lessons.description: Produce stable sorted results and avoid pagination that changes unpredictably between requests.
learningObjectives: Sort on multiple keys.
Use a unique tie-breaker for deterministic pages.
Compare OFFSET-based and keyset-style pagination conceptually.

notes.text:
SELECT order_id, order_date, status
FROM training.orders
ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC
FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY;

items: Without ORDER BY, row order is not a query contract.
OFFSET can become costly for large offsets.
Keyset pagination uses a stable last-seen key and range predicate.

quiz.question: Why add order_id after order_date in pagination?
quiz.explanation: A unique secondary ordering key stabilizes which rows fall on each page when dates tie.

summary: Stable ordering is part of reliable pagination.
A primary key is often a useful deterministic tie-breaker.

lessons.title: CASE, COALESCE, NULLIF, and Common Functions
lessons.description: Perform useful conditional and missing-value transformations close to the data.
learningObjectives: Classify rows with CASE.
Use COALESCE and NULLIF appropriately.
Recognize vendor-specific function differences.

notes.text: CASE is SQL-compliant conditional syntax. COALESCE selects the first non-NULL value; NULLIF returns NULL when its two arguments compare equal, which can be useful for avoiding division by zero when that behavior matches the business meaning.

quiz.question: What does COALESCE(a,b,c) return?
quiz.explanation: COALESCE returns the first argument that is not NULL.

summary: Conditional expressions encode data transformations clearly.
Null-handling should be designed, not improvised.

tasks.title: Build a Deterministic Customer Search
tasks.description: Write a search query with optional filters and stable ordering.
tasks.problemStatement: Search customers by name prefix and optional city, then return a stable first page.
requirements: Keep SQL structure fixed; only values should vary.
Relational database with FETCH FIRST or equivalent.
hint: A SQL client/driver supporting bound parameters.
tasks.solutionCode:
SELECT customer_id, customer_name, email, city, created_at
FROM training.customers
WHERE customer_name LIKE :prefix || '%'
  AND (:city IS NULL OR city = :city)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, customer_id DESC
FETCH FIRST :page_size ROWS ONLY;
tasks.solutionExplanation: The query uses values as parameters and adds customer_id as a deterministic tie-breaker. Placeholder syntax varies by driver, so :name is illustrative rather than a universal client syntax.

modules.title: Joins, Subqueries, Set Operations, and CTEs
modules.description: Combine tables and result sets while controlling row grain and query complexity.

lessons.title: INNER and OUTER JOINs
lessons.description: Choose joins based on which rows must survive the combination.
learningObjectives: Write explicit JOIN ... ON expressions.
Use LEFT JOIN for parent-preserving reports.
Explain row multiplication in one-to-many joins.

notes.text:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, o.order_id
FROM training.customers AS c
JOIN training.orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM training.customers AS c
LEFT JOIN training.orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name;

items: INNER JOIN keeps matching combinations.
LEFT JOIN preserves the left input and uses NULLs for unmatched right-side columns.
FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides where supported.

quiz.question: Which join keeps customers with zero orders?
options: LEFT JOIN from customers to orders
quiz.answer: LEFT JOIN from customers to orders
quiz.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves every customer while unmatched orders appear as NULL on the right.

summary: Join type encodes the population that should remain visible.
Multiplicity must be understood before calculating measures.

lessons.title: Subqueries and EXISTS
lessons.description: Use subqueries when comparison or existence is the natural form of the question.
learningObjectives: Write scalar and table subqueries.
Use EXISTS and NOT EXISTS.
Recognize correlated subqueries and their performance implications.

notes.text:
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM training.products AS p
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM training.order_items AS oi
  WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id
);
EXISTS is true when the subquery returns at least one row. The projected expression inside EXISTS does not determine truth; SELECT 1 is simply a clear conventional expression.

quiz.question: When is EXISTS TRUE?
options: When the subquery returns at least one row
Only when it returns one row
When the first column is non-NULL
quiz.answer: When the subquery returns at least one row
quiz.explanation: EXISTS is an existence predicate.

summary: EXISTS tests presence without requiring child aggregation.
Correlated subqueries can be transformed by optimizers, so performance must be checked with plans rather than assumed.

lessons.title: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT
lessons.description: Combine compatible query results with set operators.
learningObjectives: Use UNION and UNION ALL correctly.
Explain INTERSECT and EXCEPT.
Check column count and compatible types.

items: UNION eliminates duplicate result rows.
UNION ALL preserves duplicates and avoids unnecessary deduplication work.
Set inputs must be union-compatible.

quiz.question: Which operator preserves duplicates between the two inputs?
quiz.explanation: UNION ALL does not perform the duplicate elimination done by UNION.

summary: Set operators combine compatible result sets.
Choose duplicate semantics deliberately.

lessons.title: Common Table Expressions and Recursive SQL
lessons.description: Use WITH queries to decompose complex statements and traverse hierarchies.
learningObjectives: Write non-recursive CTEs.
Use multiple dependent CTEs.
Explain the anchor/recursive parts of a recursive CTE.

notes.text:
WITH customer_totals AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total_spend
  FROM training.orders o
  JOIN training.order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_name, ct.total_spend
FROM training.customers c
JOIN customer_totals ct ON ct.customer_id = c.customer_id;

WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT employee_id, manager_id, employee_name, 0 AS depth
  FROM employees
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.employee_id, e.manager_id, e.employee_name, org.depth + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org ON e.manager_id = org.employee_id
)
SELECT * FROM org;
Recursive queries require termination/cycle reasoning. A tree guarantee is different from an arbitrary graph.

quiz.question: What is the role of the anchor member in a recursive CTE?
quiz.explanation: The anchor member establishes the initial result set; the recursive member derives further rows.

summary: CTEs improve composability and readability.
Recursive CTEs make hierarchical SQL possible but require careful data guarantees.

lessons.title: Join Grain and Double-Counting
lessons.description: Diagnose inflated aggregates caused by combining multiple one-to-many relationships at once.
learningObjectives: Detect multiplicative joins.
Pre-aggregate child facts at the required grain.
Explain why apparently valid SQL can return wrong totals.

notes.text: If one order has 3 items and 2 payments, a direct join can create 6 intermediate combinations for that order. A line-item SUM performed after that join may count every item twice. Reduce each child relation to one row per order before combining them.

WITH item_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS order_total
  FROM training.order_items
  GROUP BY order_id
), payment_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid_total
  FROM training.payments
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.order_id, i.order_total, COALESCE(p.paid_total,0) AS paid_total
FROM training.orders o
JOIN item_totals i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN payment_totals p ON p.order_id = o.order_id;

quiz.question: Why can two independent child joins inflate totals?
options: The child row sets can multiply at the parent grain
quiz.answer: The child row sets can multiply at the parent grain
quiz.explanation: Each child row can combine with multiple rows from the other child relation, multiplying combinations.

summary: Correct grain is more important than clever syntax.
Pre-aggregation prevents multiplicative joins from inflating measures.

tasks.title: Repair an Inflated Order Report
tasks.description: Rewrite a report that double-counts line items because it joins two child tables at once.
tasks.problemStatement: Return one row per order with correct order value and total paid amount.
objectives: Use LEFT JOIN where missing payments should still show.
requirements: A relational database with CTE support.
Pre-aggregate items and payments independently.
SQL supporting common table expressions.
hint: Use CTEs or derived tables to reduce each child relationship first.
tasks.solutionCode:
WITH item_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS order_total
  FROM training.order_items
  GROUP BY order_id
), payment_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid_total
  FROM training.payments
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.order_id, i.order_total, COALESCE(p.paid_total, 0) AS paid_total
FROM training.orders o
JOIN item_totals i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN payment_totals p ON p.order_id = o.order_id;
tasks.solutionExplanation: Each child relation is collapsed to order grain before the final join, removing the multiplicative effect.

modules.title: Data Modification and Transaction Basics
modules.description: Change data safely and use transaction boundaries for atomic workflows.

lessons.title: INSERT and Generated Keys
lessons.description: Insert rows safely and use generated values when the implementation supports returning them.
learningObjectives: Write explicit-column INSERTs.
Load multiple rows.
Explain why returning generated values is useful.

notes.text:
-- PostgreSQL-specific
INSERT INTO training.products (product_name, category, unit_price)
VALUES ('Desk Lamp', 'Accessories', 24.00)
RETURNING product_id;
Always list target columns unless dependence on defined column order is an intentional, controlled choice.

quiz.question: Why name INSERT target columns?
options: To make the value mapping explicit
quiz.answer: To make the value mapping explicit
quiz.explanation: Explicit columns reduce accidental coupling to table column order.

summary: Explicit column lists make inserts resilient to schema changes.
RETURNING is a useful implementation feature but not universal SQL.

lessons.title: UPDATE and DELETE Safely
lessons.description: Modify data with predicates that are reviewed and recoverable.
learningObjectives: Preview an UPDATE/DELETE target with SELECT.
Use precise WHERE conditions.
Explain the risk of accidental table-wide changes.

notes.text: A missing or overly broad WHERE clause can change many rows. Use transactions and appropriate privileges for sensitive changes.

quiz.question: What should you often do before a destructive UPDATE?
options: Run a SELECT using the same predicate
quiz.answer: Run a SELECT using the same predicate
quiz.explanation: A preview query shows the rows that the modification would target.

summary: Safe DML starts with knowing the target row set.
Recovery and review matter as much as syntax.

lessons.title: Transactions, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
lessons.description: Use transactions to make related data changes behave as one recoverable unit.
learningObjectives: Open and commit/rollback transactions.
Use SAVEPOINT for checkpoints.
Explain atomicity in practical workflows.

items: ROLLBACK aborts uncommitted work.
SAVEPOINT allows partial rollback within a transaction.
Keep transactions focused and avoid leaving them open unnecessarily.

quiz.question: What does ROLLBACK do to uncommitted changes?
quiz.explanation: ROLLBACK aborts the transaction and undoes its uncommitted changes.

summary: Transactions define units of work and recovery.
Atomicity is useful for multi-step business operations.

lessons.title: MERGE and Upsert Design
lessons.description: Handle source/target synchronization while distinguishing SQL-standard-oriented MERGE from vendor-specific upsert syntax.
learningObjectives: Explain MERGE.
Write a basic MERGE statement where supported.
Understand why unique constraints and transaction semantics matter for concurrency.

notes.text:
MERGE INTO target AS t
USING source AS s
ON t.key_col = s.key_col
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET value_col = s.value_col
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (key_col, value_col)
  VALUES (s.key_col, s.value_col);
Different databases offer different upsert syntax. Use the target DBMS documentation when portability is required.

quiz.question: What problem does MERGE address?
quiz.explanation: MERGE matches source and target rows and applies configured actions such as UPDATE or INSERT.

summary: MERGE expresses conditional source/target synchronization.
Concurrency correctness is not solved by “check then insert” race-prone application logic alone.

tasks.title: Transfer Funds Atomically
tasks.description: Design a transactional transfer between two accounts.
tasks.problemStatement: Move money from one account to another without committing a partial transfer.
requirements: Relational DB supporting transactions.
Validate affected rows before committing; for concurrent workflows use appropriate locks/isolation.
hint: A transaction should contain the logical unit of work.
Production logic must also handle row counts and concurrency.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The transaction provides atomicity for the two writes. A production client must validate both updates and handle concurrency/error paths rather than blindly committing.

modules.title: Aggregation and Analytical SQL
modules.description: Build accurate summaries and row-preserving analytics with aggregates and windows.

lessons.title: GROUP BY and Aggregate Functions
lessons.description: Summarize rows at a defined grain using core aggregates.
learningObjectives: Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX.
Explain COUNT(*) versus COUNT(column).
Choose GROUP BY columns intentionally.

notes.text:
SELECT category,
       COUNT(*) AS product_count,
       AVG(unit_price) AS avg_price,
       MIN(unit_price) AS min_price,
       MAX(unit_price) AS max_price
FROM training.products
GROUP BY category;

items: COUNT(*) counts rows.
COUNT(expression) counts non-NULL expression results.
Aggregates generally skip NULL inputs where the function semantics specify that behavior.

quiz.question: What does COUNT(column) count?
quiz.explanation: COUNT(expression) counts rows where the expression is not NULL.

summary: Aggregation reduces data to a reporting grain.
NULL behavior matters for accurate measures.

lessons.title: HAVING and Conditional Aggregation
lessons.description: Filter grouped results and compute multiple conditional measures in one grouped query.
learningObjectives: Distinguish WHERE and HAVING.
Use CASE inside aggregates.
Build conditional counts/sums.

notes.text:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'PAID' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders
FROM training.orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

quiz.question: Which clause filters after grouping?
quiz.explanation: HAVING can evaluate aggregate expressions and filter grouped results.

summary: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
Conditional aggregation is a portable reporting technique.

lessons.title: Window Functions for Ranking and Row-Preserving Analytics
lessons.description: Calculate values over related rows without collapsing the result set.
learningObjectives: Use PARTITION BY and ORDER BY in OVER.
Compare ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK.
Explain how windows differ from GROUP BY.

items: ROW_NUMBER gives each row a unique sequence position.
RANK leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK does not.
Window ORDER BY controls the window calculation, not necessarily final output order.

quiz.question: Which ranking function leaves gaps after ties?
quiz.explanation: RANK assigns equal values to ties and skips subsequent rank numbers.

summary: Window functions preserve row-level detail while adding analysis.
Ranking choice should match the intended tie semantics.

lessons.title: Running Totals, LAG/LEAD, and Frames
lessons.description: Use window frames and adjacent-row functions for sequence and time-oriented analysis.
learningObjectives: Use LAG and LEAD.
Define a ROWS frame for cumulative calculations.
Recognize that window features differ slightly across DBMSs.

notes.text:
SELECT order_date,
       order_id,
       LAG(order_date) OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS previous_order,
       SUM(1) OVER (
         ORDER BY order_date, order_id
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS running_count
FROM training.orders;
Explicit frames communicate which rows belong to a cumulative calculation. This is especially useful when ordering values can tie.

quiz.question: What does LAG normally return?
options: A preceding row value in the window order
quiz.answer: A preceding row value in the window order
quiz.explanation: LAG accesses a value from an earlier row according to the window ordering and offset.

summary: LAG/LEAD compare adjacent rows in window order.
Explicit frames reduce ambiguity in running calculations.

tasks.title: Top-3 Orders per Customer
tasks.description: Return each customer’s three highest-value non-cancelled orders with customer total spend and rank.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce one row per qualifying order, preserving order detail while adding customer-level analytics.
objectives: Filter the ranking in an outer query.
requirements: PostgreSQL or another DBMS supporting window functions.
Use CTEs to establish order grain before windowing.
hint: Order amount must be computed at order grain first.
tasks.solutionCode:
WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id,
         SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS order_total
  FROM training.orders o
  JOIN training.order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
  GROUP BY o.order_id, o.customer_id
), ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
         SUM(order_total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_spend,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_total DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM order_totals
)
SELECT *
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY customer_id, rn;
tasks.solutionExplanation: The first CTE fixes the order grain, the second adds window calculations, and the outer query filters ranked rows.

modules.title: Reusable and Advanced SQL Constructs
modules.description: Use recursive CTEs, views, routines, and triggers deliberately.

lessons.title: Recursive Hierarchies
lessons.description: Traverse organizational or category trees with recursive CTEs.
learningObjectives: Build an anchor and recursive member.
Track depth.
Reason about cycles and termination.

notes.text:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT category_id, parent_id, name, 0 AS depth
  FROM category
  WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.category_id, c.parent_id, c.name, tree.depth + 1
  FROM category c
  JOIN tree ON c.parent_id = tree.category_id
)
SELECT * FROM tree ORDER BY depth, category_id;
This pattern assumes a tree. Graphs with cycles require cycle detection or bounded traversal.

quiz.question: What starts a recursive CTE?
quiz.explanation: The anchor supplies initial rows before recursive derivation begins.

summary: Recursive SQL is a structured form of repeated row derivation.
Hierarchy correctness depends on data constraints as well as query logic.

lessons.title: Views as Abstraction and Access Boundaries
lessons.description: Encapsulate complex queries in reusable interfaces.
learningObjectives: Create a view.
Explain view dependencies.
Use a view with privileges to expose only approved data.

notes.text:
CREATE VIEW training.customer_activity AS
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM training.customers c
LEFT JOIN training.orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name;
A normal PostgreSQL view stores a query definition. Views can also reduce coupling for consumers and can work as a privilege boundary when underlying tables are not directly granted.

quiz.question: What is a practical benefit of a view?
quiz.explanation: A view can provide a stable, reusable query interface over underlying relations.

summary: Views are query contracts, not automatically cached result sets.
Access-control design and view design can complement one another.

lessons.title: SQL Functions and Procedures
lessons.description: Package reusable database-side logic while distinguishing function and procedure semantics.
learningObjectives: Create a SQL function with arguments.
Explain return types and result sets.
Distinguish functions from procedures.

notes.text: PostgreSQL supports SQL-language functions and procedures. Exact routine syntax, transaction-control capabilities, and procedural languages are implementation-specific.

quiz.question: How is a PostgreSQL procedure invoked?
quiz.explanation: PostgreSQL procedures are invoked with CALL.

summary: Routines can centralize repeated data logic.
Routine behavior should be documented because execution happens inside the database.

lessons.title: Triggers and Hidden Side Effects
lessons.description: Automate database reactions while learning when triggers help and when they increase complexity.
learningObjectives: Explain BEFORE and AFTER triggers.
Use NEW/OLD in row-level triggers.
Assess trigger side effects and debugging costs.

notes.text: Triggers are implicit control flow: a write can cause additional work that is not visible in the calling SQL text. Keep them small and documented.

quiz.question: Can a PostgreSQL BEFORE row trigger modify NEW before the row is written?
quiz.explanation: PostgreSQL permits BEFORE row-level triggers to modify the NEW record.

summary: Triggers can automate cross-cutting behavior.
Hidden behavior increases operational and debugging complexity.

tasks.title: Create a Customer Reporting View
tasks.description: Expose customer activity through a view without changing base tables.
tasks.problemStatement: Return one row per customer with total orders, last order date, and lifetime non-cancelled value.
requirements: PostgreSQL or another DBMS with views.
Use LEFT JOIN for inactive customers.
SQL supporting CREATE VIEW.
hint: Aggregate order facts at customer grain first.
tasks.solutionCode:
CREATE VIEW training.customer_activity AS
WITH totals AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id,
         COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count,
         MAX(o.order_date) AS last_order_date,
         SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS lifetime_value
  FROM training.orders o
  JOIN training.order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name,
       COALESCE(t.order_count,0) AS order_count,
       t.last_order_date,
       COALESCE(t.lifetime_value,0) AS lifetime_value
FROM training.customers c
LEFT JOIN totals t ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id;
tasks.solutionExplanation: The CTE establishes customer grain before the outer LEFT JOIN, preventing order-line multiplication and preserving customers without activity.

modules.title: Transactions and Concurrency
modules.description: Advance from atomic transactions to isolation levels, locking, and retry-aware design.

lessons.title: ACID and Transaction Invariants
lessons.description: Connect transaction guarantees to actual business invariants.
learningObjectives: Explain atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability.
Differentiate database-enforced consistency from application business logic.

items: Atomicity: the transaction commits as a unit or aborts.
Consistency: successful work respects the configured integrity rules and the intended transaction logic.
Isolation: concurrent transactions observe data according to the chosen isolation behavior.
Durability: committed work persists according to the DBMS/storage durability design.

quiz.question: Which ACID property is the all-or-nothing property?
quiz.explanation: Atomicity makes a transaction indivisible from the perspective of commit/abort outcome.

summary: ACID describes system guarantees, not a substitute for correct business logic.
Constraints and transactions work together to preserve invariants.

lessons.title: Isolation Levels and Concurrency Anomalies
lessons.description: Reason about dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, phantoms, and serialization anomalies.
learningObjectives: Compare common isolation levels.
Explain PostgreSQL’s Read Committed and Serializable behavior.
Design retry logic for serialization failures.

notes.text: The SQL standard defines four isolation levels. PostgreSQL exposes their names but implements Read Uncommitted like Read Committed. PostgreSQL Repeatable Read is stronger than the minimum standard requirement for phantom protection. Serializable may abort a transaction with a serialization failure, so applications must be prepared to retry the whole transaction.

quiz.question: Which isolation level is the strictest?
quiz.explanation: Serializable aims to provide behavior equivalent to some serial order of committed transactions.

summary: Isolation is a concurrency contract, not merely a performance knob.
Retrying the whole logical transaction is important after serialization failure.

lessons.title: Explicit Row Locking
lessons.description: Coordinate read-modify-write workflows with targeted row locks.
learningObjectives: Use SELECT FOR UPDATE.
Explain lock scope.
Reduce deadlock risk with consistent lock ordering.

notes.text: Locks can increase contention. Keep transactions short and lock only rows necessary for the invariant being protected.

quiz.question: Why lock rows in a transfer workflow?
quiz.explanation: Row locks can serialize conflicting access to specific rows within the transaction.

summary: Explicit locking can protect critical read-modify-write sequences.
Deadlock prevention often includes a consistent acquisition order.

tasks.title: Serializable Booking with Retry
tasks.description: Design a reservation transaction that retries after serialization failure.
tasks.problemStatement: Two concurrent sessions may attempt to reserve the same resource. Use Serializable isolation and rerun the full transaction after an abort.
requirements: PostgreSQL or another DBMS with Serializable isolation.
Retry the entire transaction, not one statement.
DBMS transaction support.
hint: The retry loop belongs in the application or suitable procedure layer.
tasks.solutionExplanation: When the transaction ends with a serialization failure, the client must discard the aborted transaction and start the complete logical operation again.

modules.title: SQL Performance and Query Plans
modules.description: Tune SQL with indexes, execution plans, statistics, and evidence-based rewrites.

lessons.title: Indexes and Their Trade-offs
lessons.description: Treat indexes as workload-driven access paths.
learningObjectives: Explain why indexes can speed selective searches.
Recognize write/storage costs.
Choose candidate indexes from query patterns.

notes.text:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_date
ON training.orders (customer_id, order_date);

items: B-tree indexes cover many equality/range/order patterns.
Indexes add storage and maintenance cost on writes.
Index every-column thinking is usually wasteful; verify with workload evidence.

quiz.question: What is a cost of unnecessary indexes?
quiz.explanation: Indexes need maintenance and storage, so excess indexes can hurt write performance and resource use.

summary: Indexes are physical-design decisions driven by queries.
The optimal set is a balance between reads, writes, and storage.

lessons.title: Composite, Partial, and Expression Indexes
lessons.description: Design specialized indexes when ordinary single-column indexing does not match the workload.
learningObjectives: Explain composite index column order.
Use partial indexes for relevant row subsets.
Use expression indexes for matching computed predicates.

notes.text: Composite index order matters. A partial index covers only rows satisfying its predicate. An expression index matches queries written against the same expression in systems that support the feature.

quiz.question: What is a partial index?
options: An index over rows satisfying a predicate
An index with one column only
An index that cannot be used by SELECT
quiz.answer: An index over rows satisfying a predicate
quiz.explanation: A partial index stores entries only for rows meeting its definition predicate.

summary: Specialized indexes should be justified by real predicates and access paths.
Advanced index features are often vendor-specific.

lessons.title: EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE
lessons.description: Read execution plans instead of guessing at performance problems.
learningObjectives: Use EXPLAIN.
Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE safely.
Compare estimated and actual row counts.

notes.text:
EXPLAIN
SELECT order_id, order_date
FROM training.orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY order_date DESC;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT order_id, order_date
FROM training.orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY order_date DESC;
EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. Use caution with data-changing statements and production workloads.

quiz.question: What does EXPLAIN show?
quiz.explanation: EXPLAIN exposes the plan selected or proposed by the optimizer.

summary: Execution plans are evidence about optimizer choices.
A sequential scan is not automatically bad; context and data size matter.

lessons.title: Statistics, Sargability, and Query Rewrites
lessons.description: Use measurements and planner evidence to refine SQL.
learningObjectives: Explain why predicates can be easier or harder to optimize.
Understand the relationship between statistics and cardinality estimates.
Compare before/after plans instead of claiming unmeasured speedups.

notes.text:
-- Range predicate that directly constrains the indexed column
SELECT *
FROM training.customers
WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01'
  AND created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2026-02-01';

-- May require an expression index in some systems
SELECT *
FROM training.customers
WHERE LOWER(email) = 'user@example.com';

Sargability is an optimizer-oriented concept: a predicate is easier to optimize when the search condition can use an available access path. Exact behavior depends on the DBMS, statistics, indexes, and query plan.

quiz.question: Why can LOWER(email) change index usage?
options: The expression changes the searchable form of the column
quiz.answer: The expression changes the searchable form of the column
quiz.explanation: An ordinary index on email does not automatically equal an index on LOWER(email); some systems support expression indexes for this use.

summary: Performance tuning is empirical.
Rewrite only when the plan or measurement provides evidence.

tasks.title: Tune a Lowercase Email Lookup
tasks.description: Use EXPLAIN to choose a suitable index for a case-normalized lookup.
tasks.problemStatement: Compare the plan before and after adding an expression index for LOWER(email).
objectives: Explain when the planner might still choose another plan.
requirements: PostgreSQL recommended.
Match the index expression to the query predicate.
PostgreSQL index and EXPLAIN support.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The expression index matches the search expression. Whether it is chosen depends on table size, statistics, costs, and the actual data distribution; the assignment requires evidence from the plan rather than a fabricated benchmark.

modules.title: SQL Security and Safe Query Construction
modules.description: Protect SQL-driven systems with parameterization, least privilege, and controlled dynamic SQL.

lessons.title: SQL Injection and Parameterization
lessons.description: Understand SQL injection as a query-construction flaw and use parameterized queries as the primary defense for values.
learningObjectives: Explain code/data separation in SQL queries.
Use bound parameters.
Recognize why escaping is a weaker primary strategy.

notes.text: Never concatenate untrusted input into SQL command text. Bind it as a parameter using the application driver.

quiz.question: What is the primary defense for untrusted SQL values?
quiz.explanation: Parameterized interfaces keep data values separate from executable SQL structure.

summary: Parameterization keeps SQL structure separate from user data.
OWASP recommends parameterized queries as the primary defense.

lessons.title: Roles, Privileges, and Least Privilege
lessons.description: Limit database capabilities according to workload needs.
learningObjectives: Explain ownership and GRANT/REVOKE.
Design a read-only role.
Use views as narrow interfaces where appropriate.

notes.text: Do not put real passwords in course code or source control. Use an external secret mechanism for credentials.

quiz.question: What is least privilege?
options: Each identity gets only the access needed for its role
quiz.answer: Each identity gets only the access needed for its role
quiz.explanation: Least privilege limits unnecessary permissions and reduces impact from mistakes or compromise.

summary: Least privilege reduces blast radius.
Grant access to the narrowest object set that satisfies the workload.

lessons.title: Safe Dynamic SQL and Identifier Allow-Lists
lessons.description: Handle cases where query structure must vary without treating untrusted identifiers as safe data values.
learningObjectives: Distinguish values from identifiers.
Design allow-lists for sorting/column choices.
Explain why arbitrary identifier concatenation is risky.

notes.text:
-- Example fixed choices chosen by application logic:
-- "name" -> customer_name
-- "city" -> city
-- "newest" -> created_at DESC

SELECT customer_id, customer_name, city, created_at
FROM training.customers
ORDER BY created_at DESC;

Bind parameters normally represent values. Table/column names and sort-direction syntax often require controlled SQL construction or database-specific identifier APIs; OWASP recommends allow-list validation for such structural inputs.

quiz.question: Why can’t a normal bind parameter replace a column name?
options: Bind parameters normally represent values, not SQL identifiers
Columns are not part of SQL
quiz.answer: Bind parameters normally represent values, not SQL identifiers
quiz.explanation: The prepared-statement interface binds data values; structural identifiers require separate safe handling.

summary: Dynamic SQL should separate data values from SQL structure.
Allow-listing keeps structural variation constrained to known-good fragments.

tasks.title: Secure a Customer Search Query
tasks.description: Replace unsafe dynamic SQL with parameters and a fixed sort allow-list.
tasks.problemStatement: A search endpoint accepts a name fragment and a sort option; redesign it without concatenating raw user input into SQL.
requirements: SQL driver with bound parameters.
Never let raw user text become an identifier or SQL fragment.
Relational database and application client.
hint: The sort option must be mapped by application code to one of a small set of known expressions.
tasks.solutionCode:
SELECT customer_id, customer_name, city, created_at
FROM training.customers
WHERE customer_name ILIKE '%' || :name_fragment || '%'
ORDER BY created_at DESC;
tasks.solutionExplanation: The name fragment is a bound value. The application maps the requested sort option to a predetermined ORDER BY fragment instead of concatenating the raw option.

modules.title: Testing, Recovery, and Large-Table Design
modules.description: Make SQL work repeatable and operationally safer with testing, recovery practices, and physical design awareness.

lessons.title: Repeatable SQL Testing
lessons.description: Test database behavior with controlled fixtures and assertions.
learningObjectives: Create deterministic fixtures.
Test positive and negative cases.
Use transactions/disposable schemas for cleanup.

items: Test constraints with invalid input, not only successful paths.
Assert expected rows/values instead of only checking for absence of exceptions.

quiz.question: Why include negative constraint tests?
options: To verify invalid states are rejected
quiz.answer: To verify invalid states are rejected
quiz.explanation: Negative tests exercise the database rules that protect integrity.

summary: Repeatability is essential for useful database tests.
Failure cases verify that constraints actually protect the domain.

lessons.title: Backup, Restore, and Migration Discipline
lessons.description: Treat database recovery and schema evolution as operational engineering.
learningObjectives: Explain logical backup at a high level.
Design ordered migrations.
Distinguish backup existence from verified recoverability.

notes.text:
-- PostgreSQL command-line tooling (not SQL statements)
pg_dump -Fc training_db > training_db.dump
createdb training_db_restore
pg_restore -d training_db_restore training_db.dump
A backup is not a recovery plan until restore procedures are tested in an environment that resembles the target failure/recovery scenario.

quiz.question: What verifies that a backup is actually usable for recovery?
quiz.explanation: A tested restore demonstrates that the backup can actually be used to recover the intended state.

summary: Migrations change state over time; backups support recovery.
Restore testing validates the recovery path.

lessons.title: Partitioning and Large-Table Design
lessons.description: Recognize when partitioning can improve manageability and query behavior for large tables.
learningObjectives: Explain range partitioning.
Choose a partition key from workload/lifecycle needs.
Distinguish partitioning from indexing and sharding.

notes.text: Partitioning creates one logical table with data distributed across partitions. It is especially useful when data lifecycle and query predicates naturally align with a partition key. It is not a universal performance solution.

quiz.question: What is a strong reason to partition time-oriented data?
options: Align storage/lifecycle with the time dimension
quiz.answer: Align storage/lifecycle with the time dimension
quiz.explanation: Partitioning can help when data lifecycle, retention, and access patterns align with the partition key.

summary: Partitioning is a physical data-layout choice.
Partition pruning and maintenance benefits depend on workload and design.

tasks.title: Build a Repeatable SQL Regression Suite
tasks.description: Create a database test script that validates key queries and integrity rules without leaving fixture data.
tasks.problemStatement: The suite must insert controlled fixtures, assert expected results, test at least two invalid states, and leave no test rows afterward.
requirements: Use expected-error checks in the surrounding test runner for statements that should fail.
PostgreSQL recommended; command-line or test-runner execution.
hint: A transaction is useful for fixture isolation.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The transaction isolates the fixture. Expected-error checks should be handled by the test runner so that a deliberate constraint failure does not abort the whole test script unexpectedly.

modules.title: Final Project: Library Lending Analytics Database
modules.description: A realistic SQL capstone that combines schema design, integrity, querying, analytics, security, and performance inspection. This is the final practical assessment and is assessed as one integrated project rather than separate difficulty-tier tasks.

lessons.title: Capstone Build and Review
lessons.description: Execute the full library lending system and defend the design choices in schema, queries, indexes, security, and testing.
learningObjectives: Build the schema and load the fixture data.
Validate constraints with positive and negative tests.
Run and explain each report at its intended grain.
Interpret the EXPLAIN plan and connect it to index design.
Verify the reporting role has only required access.
Identify at least two PostgreSQL-specific features that would need review for portability.

notes.text: Implementation steps

items: Create a clean PostgreSQL database and run schema.sql.
Load data.sql and verify row counts.
Run constraint-failure tests without leaving invalid data.
Execute reports.sql and document the result grain.
Capture the EXPLAIN output for the open-loan query.
Run audit.sql in a controlled lab and verify read-only access.
Write a portability note comparing the project to another SQL implementation.

notes.text:
This capstone builds a library lending system as a relational SQL design. The schema demonstrates identity keys, UNIQUE/CHECK constraints, foreign keys, defaults, composite indexes, a PostgreSQL partial index, and clear entity/relationship grain.

The reporting layer combines joins, a LEFT JOIN, CTEs, EXISTS, aggregation, and a window ranking query. The open-loan partial index is tied to a real reporting predicate and is inspected with EXPLAIN rather than justified by an invented benchmark. The reporting role and view demonstrate least privilege and a narrow read interface.

The project intentionally labels PostgreSQL-specific features: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, FILTER, partial indexes, and EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Portability review is part of the assessment so students learn to distinguish SQL concepts from DBMS-specific syntax.

practicals.title: Build and Audit the Library Database
practicals.description: Execute the capstone end-to-end and review the technical decisions.
steps: Exercise constraint failures in a controlled transaction/test harness.
Run audit.sql in a lab database.
Capture and explain the execution plan.
practicals.solution:
{
  "schema.sql": "CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS library;

CREATE TABLE library.member (
  member_id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  full_name VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
  email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  joined_on DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE,
  active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE
);

CREATE TABLE library.book (
  book_id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  isbn VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  title VARCHAR(250) NOT NULL,
  category VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
  published_year INTEGER CHECK (published_year BETWEEN 1400 AND 2100),
  total_copies INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (total_copies >= 0),
  available_copies INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (available_copies BETWEEN 0 AND total_copies)
);

CREATE TABLE library.loan (
  loan_id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  member_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES library.member(member_id),
  book_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES library.book(book_id),
  loaned_on DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE,
  due_on DATE NOT NULL,
  returned_on DATE,
  CHECK (due_on >= loaned_on),
  CHECK (returned_on IS NULL OR returned_on >= loaned_on)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_loan_member_due
  ON library.loan (member_id, due_on DESC);

CREATE INDEX idx_loan_open_book
  ON library.loan (book_id)
  WHERE returned_on IS NULL;
",
  "data.sql": "INSERT INTO library.member(full_name, email)
VALUES
('Member One', 'member1@example.test'),
('Member Four', 'member2@example.test'),
('Member Three', 'member3@example.test');

INSERT INTO library.book(isbn, title, category, published_year, total_copies, available_copies)
VALUES
('9780000000001', 'Relational Database Design', 'Database', 2022, 4, 3),
('9780000000002', 'SQL Query Patterns', 'Database', 2024, 5, 5),
('9780000000003', 'Systems Thinking', 'Technology', 2021, 3, 2),
('9780000000004', 'Data Modeling in Practice', 'Database', 2023, 2, 2);

INSERT INTO library.loan(member_id, book_id, loaned_on, due_on, returned_on)
VALUES
(1,1,DATE '2026-01-10',DATE '2026-01-24',DATE '2026-01-20'),
(1,2,DATE '2026-02-03',DATE '2026-02-17',NULL),
(2,1,DATE '2026-02-05',DATE '2026-02-19',NULL),
(2,3,DATE '2026-01-12',DATE '2026-01-26',DATE '2026-01-25'),
(3,4,DATE '2026-02-01',DATE '2026-02-15',NULL);
",
  "reports.sql": "SELECT l.loan_id, m.full_name, b.title, l.loaned_on, l.due_on,
       CURRENT_DATE - l.due_on AS days_from_due
FROM library.loan l
JOIN library.member m ON m.member_id = l.member_id
JOIN library.book b ON b.book_id = l.book_id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL
ORDER BY l.due_on, l.loan_id;

WITH member_stats AS (
  SELECT m.member_id, m.full_name,
         COUNT(l.loan_id) AS total_loans,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL) AS open_loans,
         MAX(l.loaned_on) AS last_loan_date
  FROM library.member m
  LEFT JOIN library.loan l ON l.member_id = m.member_id
  GROUP BY m.member_id, m.full_name
)
SELECT * FROM member_stats
ORDER BY total_loans DESC, member_id;

WITH book_counts AS (
  SELECT b.book_id, b.title, COUNT(l.loan_id) AS loan_count
  FROM library.book b
  LEFT JOIN library.loan l ON l.book_id = b.book_id
  GROUP BY b.book_id, b.title
)
SELECT title, loan_count,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY loan_count DESC) AS demand_rank
FROM book_counts
ORDER BY demand_rank, title;

SELECT b.book_id, b.title
FROM library.book b
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM library.loan l WHERE l.book_id = b.book_id
)
ORDER BY b.book_id;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT loan_id, member_id, book_id, due_on
FROM library.loan
WHERE returned_on IS NULL AND book_id = 1;
",
  "audit.sql": "CREATE ROLE library_reporter;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA library TO library_reporter;
CREATE VIEW library.member_activity AS
SELECT m.member_id,
       m.full_name,
       COUNT(l.loan_id) AS loan_count,
       MAX(l.loaned_on) AS last_loan_date
FROM library.member m
LEFT JOIN library.loan l ON l.member_id = m.member_id
GROUP BY m.member_id, m.full_name;

GRANT SELECT ON library.member_activity TO library_reporter;
"
}
practicals.output: The result is a working library schema, populated data, operational/analytical reports, an inspectable execution plan, and a narrow reporting role/view.

quiz.question: Which artifact best demonstrates performance reasoning?
options: Using EXPLAIN to connect the query plan to index design
quiz.answer: Using EXPLAIN to connect the query plan to index design
quiz.explanation: Performance work should be based on optimizer evidence and representative workload data.

summary: The capstone integrates the course’s core SQL skills in one coherent domain.
A successful submission includes both working SQL and an explanation of why the design is appropriate.

         MAX(l.loaned_on) AS last_loan_date
  FROM library.member m
  LEFT JOIN library.loan l ON l.member_id = m.member_id
  GROUP BY m.member_id, m.full_name
)
SELECT * FROM member_stats
ORDER BY total_loans DESC, member_id;

WITH book_counts AS (
  SELECT b.book_id, b.title, COUNT(l.loan_id) AS loan_count
  FROM library.book b
  LEFT JOIN library.loan l ON l.book_id = b.book_id
  GROUP BY b.book_id, b.title
)
SELECT title, loan_count,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY loan_count DESC) AS demand_rank
FROM book_counts
ORDER BY demand_rank, title;

SELECT b.book_id, b.title
FROM library.book b
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM library.loan l WHERE l.book_id = b.book_id
)
ORDER BY b.book_id;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT loan_id, member_id, book_id, due_on
FROM library.loan
WHERE returned_on IS NULL AND book_id = 1;

project.explanation:
This capstone builds a library lending system as a relational SQL design. The schema demonstrates identity keys, UNIQUE/CHECK constraints, foreign keys, defaults, composite indexes, a PostgreSQL partial index, and clear entity/relationship grain.

The reporting layer combines joins, a LEFT JOIN, CTEs, EXISTS, aggregation, and a window ranking query. The open-loan partial index is tied to a real reporting predicate and is inspected with EXPLAIN rather than justified by an invented benchmark. The reporting role and view demonstrate least privilege and a narrow read interface.

The project intentionally labels PostgreSQL-specific features: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, FILTER, partial indexes, and EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Portability review is part of the assessment so students learn to distinguish SQL concepts from DBMS-specific syntax.
